cases.quote: For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: §A.4 lists the question mark as UCS 003F and prints ？ in its Character column, and the §A preamble Note quoted above says why the two columns differ: the document lists the script-neutral code point and real Japanese text carries the compatibility counterpart. §3.9.2's own example list for cl-04 is written ？！ — U+FF1F and U+FF01, the compatibility pair, not U+003F and U+0021 — so the section that establishes the classification illustrates it with exactly the occurrence this case supplies. An implementation that keys Appendix A by code point without folding the Wide decomposition answers nothing for the commonest form of this mark in Japanese text, and does so silently.

forbidden.why: §A.27 lists 003F QUESTION MARK with the Remark 'proportionally-spaced'. U+FF1F is the full-width compatibility counterpart and the item declares the ideographic frame, so the cl-27 listing is not the one that describes this occurrence.

cases.rationale: The first row of §A.4, quoted above in the document's own column order — Character, UCS, Name, Common name. Its fifth column, Remarks 備考, is empty in both the English and the Japanese rendering, so §A.4 states no frame, no writing-direction restriction and no role for this member; the row is an unconditional listing. The item is the second occurrence of the input §3.9.2 writes as its cl-04 example, which is also why this case and the one above share one input: a case is one input and several questions about it.

cases.quote: ⁉ 2049 EXCLAMATION QUESTION MARK 感嘆符疑問符
cases.rationale: The last row of §A.4. U+2049 is named by cl-04 and by no other Appendix A table, so nothing has to be separated and the frame axis decides nothing here; the answer is the listing itself. This case and the one below it supply the same member on two different frames and expect byte-identical answers, which is what §A.4's empty Remarks column means, stated as something an implementation can fail.

cases.quote: ⁉ 2049 EXCLAMATION QUESTION MARK 感嘆符疑問符
cases.rationale: The same member on the proportional frame, with an advance a proportional font would report, and the same expected answer. The Remarks column is the axis Appendix A uses to separate two listings of one code point — §A.27's rows carry 'proportionally-spaced', §A.5's semicolon carries 'used in horizontal composition' — and all six of §A.4's Remarks cells are literally empty in both locales. No other table lists U+2049, so no listing competes with §A.4's and there is nothing for a declared frame to select between. An implementation that routes a proportionally-set non-Japanese-looking glyph to cl-27 by the frame alone, rather than by what Appendix A lists, passes the case above and fails this one.

forbidden.why: §A.27 does not list 2049. A frame is what separates two listings of one code point; it never creates a listing Appendix A does not have.

cases.quote: ‼ 203C DOUBLE EXCLAMATION MARK 感嘆符二つ
cases.rationale: §A.4 holds six keys and every one of them is a single code point: this class contains no code-point sequence, unlike §A.27, which lists <02E5, 02E9> and <02E9, 02E5> as two distinct members. U+203C is therefore one occurrence keyed by one code point, and not the sequence <0021, 0021> under another name. An implementation that normalizes U+203C to two exclamation marks before classifying reports two occurrences where the document has one, and every downstream count — items on the line, break opportunities, adjacencies against the two matrices — is then off by one.

The converse of the case above, on the same input. The two exclamation marks that follow U+203C are two occurrences of one key and not one occurrence of a two-code-point key, because §A.4 has no two-code-point key to match them against. The input is the assertion: a stream whose items cut an Appendix A key in half is refused rather than misclassified, so the fact that this three-item stream is well-formed is the fact that nothing in cl-04 spans items 1 and 2.

cases.quote: ⁇ 2047 DOUBLE QUESTION MARK 疑問符二つ
cases.rationale: This item declares no frame at all, and the answer is still the listing. Two facts meet here and both are §A.4's. U+2047 is named by cl-04 alone, so there is no second candidate an unstated frame would leave undecided; and §A.4 is none of the five classes whose members must declare a frame, because §3.1.2 states the half-width advance of cl-01, cl-02, cl-05, cl-06 and cl-07 and says nothing about cl-04. A caller who holds no frame for this occurrence is therefore not obliged to invent one, which is not true of the full stop beside it.

cases.quote: There are some cases where dividing punctuation marks (cl-04) are used in the middle of a sentence, not at the end. In those cases, either add no spacing or a quarter em spacing before and after the dividing punctuation mark see Figure 74).
cases.rationale: The quoted Note is the only place JLReq distinguishes two jobs a cl-04 occurrence can have, and what it varies is the spacing on both sides — one em after a sentence-final mark, solid or a quarter em around a sentence-medial one. It does not vary the class, and §A.4 lists no member twice. So an occurrence declaring the sentence-medial role is cl-04 exactly as a sentence-final one is, and an implementation that reads the role as a class selector answers a class for a distinction the document spends on an amount. The quote carries the published document's own punctuation, including the unbalanced parenthesis in 'mark see Figure 74)'.

permitted.source: JLReq (3.1.6 Note 3, the quarter em reading)

cases.quote: Breaking a line is allowed before or after the following character classes even though Table 2 prohibits it.
cases.rationale: §C.3's Very loose (Newspapers) level lists Dividing punctuation marks (cl-04) under the sentence quoted above, and the sentence says what kind of relaxation it is: an override of Table 2, granted before or after the class. It is a break permission and not a change of class — it names cl-04 in order to relax the class, which presupposes that the occurrence is still in it. So the answer is cl-04 at every level, and the two entries below say so: an implementation that reaches the newspaper level by moving cl-04 into some breakable class answers 4 under the empty overlay and something else under the very-loose one, and fails on the second. That is the mechanism question §C.2 notes 1 to 3 answer the other way, where the document does say 'shall be treated as a member of'.

permitted.source: JLReq (A.4), at the Strict level Policy::JLREQ selects

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: U+203D INTERROBANG is a question mark and an exclamation mark in one glyph, which is what four of §A.4's six members are, and §A.4 does not list it. That is not an exclusion. §A scopes every one of its tables to the non-ideographic characters of ISO/IEC 10646 collections 285 and 286, and the sentence quoted above records that JIS X 4051 leaves the handling of a character its lists do not mention implementation-defined, and that JLReq inherits that position. So the boundary of cl-04 is drawn by the collection the tables enumerate rather than by a judgment about the mark, and an answer here is a published reading and never a requirement — which is why this case's standing is unstated and both readings are recorded. On the ideographic frame the two agree, and the case below is where they part.

permitted.source: The unconditional reading: every unlisted occurrence is cl-19

forbidden.why: §A.4 lists six keys and U+203D is not one of them. A reading that adds an unlisted mark to the class it resembles is the one thing §3.9.2 does not license: it records that the question is implementation-defined, not that the answer is the nearest table.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: The same unlisted mark set with a proportional font, which is where the two readings of §3.9.2's silence differ and therefore where both have to be published. The by-frame reading extends the one distinction JLReq itself draws over text its tables do not enumerate — §3.2.4 sets full-width and fixed-width Western characters as quasi Japanese characters, §3.2.6 gives proportionally set Western text the composition rules of cl-27 — and answers cl-27 here. The unconditional reading answers cl-19 on every frame. Neither is stated by the document, so the case records both with the choice that selects each, and an implementation is scored against the one it declares rather than against ours.

permitted.source: The unconditional reading: every unlisted occurrence is cl-19
